welcome.card: Discovery, Reach Pages, forms, data, accessibility, and secure handoff for nonprofit clients.
welcome.intro: Technical consulting at PVV is mostly about choosing simple, free tools a client can keep running without you. Under the constitution, that means websites, surveys, forms, data pipelines, and technical advice that makes a nonprofit's operations more efficient. This training uses one practice client throughout.
welcome.outcome: A client intake, a Reach Page plan, a form design, a data layout, an accessibility check, and an account inventory, all built for a practice client and ready to reuse.

modules.title: Your role and discovery

blocks.x: The most common technical mistake is building something the client didn't need, can't maintain, or already had. Discovery prevents that, and it comes before any building.

blocks.title: Five questions before any build
blocks.x: What problem are we solving? Who will use it? Who maintains it after PVV leaves? What's the timeline? What's the budget? ($0 is the default.)

head: Need
Use this (free)
rows: The client's existing donation tool, or a simple payment link

blocks.x: Our default is Google Sites + Google Forms + Google Sheets. The client probably already has Gmail, nothing needs coding, and you can hand it off in about 15 minutes.

blocks.title: Red flags
blocks.x: "We need an app" usually means a form. "Make it like a big nonprofit's site" means a budget you don't have. "We need it Friday" when it's Wednesday means too much. No one on their team who can update content means it will go stale.

blocks.title: Bridge Kit: what PVV has already built
blocks.why: Skim how a client's Reach Page and tracking console are structured.

options: A native iPhone and Android app

options: Which framework is trendiest?

blocks.explain: If nobody can maintain it, it will go stale.

modules.title: Build the Reach Page

blocks.x: The Reach Page is the centerpiece of PVV's Bridge Kit: one mobile-friendly page where someone can volunteer, donate, or learn more in under two minutes. Most visitors will be on a phone, so design for that first.

blocks.caption: Everything else can wait. The 5-second test: a new visitor gets all three at a glance.
legend: Mission: what you do and who you help

blocks.title: The 5-second test
blocks.x: A new visitor should understand what the organization does, who it helps, and what they can do, within five seconds of landing.

items: Intake: collect the logo, photos, and copy.
Draft the copy in a Google Doc, where the client edits, not in the site builder.
Build the pages, embed forms, and add alt text to every image.
Test on a phone. Click every link and submit every form.
Get client approval, publish, and write the handoff doc.

modules.title: Forms and surveys

blocks.x: A good form replaces a paper stack and feeds a spreadsheet directly. You're often collecting information from vulnerable people, so ask for less, not more.

items: Only ask what you need. Every field is a privacy risk and a reason to quit.
Use dropdowns and checkboxes instead of free text, so the data stays clean.
Add a consent checkbox, such as "I agree to be contacted."
Write a clear confirmation message that says what happens next.
For surveys, allow anonymous responses unless you truly need names.
Share the response sheet with named people only, never "anyone with the link."

modules.title: Data and spreadsheets

blocks.x: Most PVV data work follows one simple pipeline. Keep it simple and you can hand it off in minutes.

blocks.caption: The standard pipeline, entirely in the client's own Google account.

items: One row per record, one value per cell. No merged cells.
Use dropdowns or data validation for categories, so "Mon," "monday," and "M" can't all appear.
Use one date format everywhere.
Leave the raw responses tab alone. Do your cleaning and counting in a separate tab.

blocks.title: A three-tab master sheet
blocks.x: Responses: raw form data, never edited by hand. Working: the cleaned copy. Dashboard: the two or three numbers the client reports each month.

blocks.title: How to use Google Forms (see the section on responses in a Sheet)
blocks.why: A form can send its responses straight to a Sheet.

fields.label: Name three tabs for a volunteer-tracking sheet and say what each one holds.
Name one metric the client will report every month.

blocks.q: An "Availability" column contains "Mon," "monday," and "M." What fixes this at the source?
options: Clean it by hand every month
Use a dropdown or checkbox question in the form
Leave it as is
blocks.explain: Prevent messy data on the way in rather than cleaning it later.
blocks.hint: Fix the cause, not the symptom.

blocks.q: Which tab should people edit by hand?
options: The raw Responses tab
The Working tab
The Dashboard tab
blocks.explain: The raw tab stays untouched so you can always start over.
blocks.hint: Which tab is your safety net?

checklist: I described a three-tab master sheet

modules.title: Accessibility and mobile

blocks.x: Accessible design helps people with disabilities, and it also helps anyone on a small phone, in bright sun, or on a slow connection. For PVV clients, whose communities often rely on phones, it's not optional.

head: Check
How
rows: At least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Check with a contrast checker.
Add short, meaningful alt text. Decorative images get empty alt text.
Every field has a visible label.
Say where they go. "Volunteer sign-up," not "click here."
Open the page on a real phone and try every button.

modules.title: Security, privacy, and handoff

blocks.x: You'll often handle information about vulnerable people. The client owns that data, and your job is to protect it and then hand everything back cleanly.

items: Keep client data in the client's accounts, not your personal one.
Share sheets with named people only, never "anyone with the link."
Never discuss individuals' personal information in PVV meetings.
Use long, unique passwords with a password manager, and turn on multifactor authentication.
Never put passwords, tokens, or API keys in a public GitHub repo. Keep them in environment variables.

blocks.x: Every project ends with a one-page guide for the client: how to check new form responses, how to edit the site's text, how to update the donate link, and who to contact if something breaks. Include an inventory of every account, who owns it, and who can access it.

blocks.why: How to find the setting in any account.

blocks.intro: Create a one-page handoff guide in Google Docs for your practice client, including the account inventory. Set sharing to Anyone with the link can view (use no real client data), then paste the link. Your category chair will review it.

blocks.q: Where should a client's form response data live?
options: In your personal Google account, so you can forward it
In a public sheet anyone can view
In the client's Google account, with access limited to named people
blocks.explain: The client owns the data, and access should be limited.

blocks.q: Which belongs in a handoff document?
options: Your personal passwords
How to read responses, edit text, update the donate link, and who to contact
Nothing. The client will figure it out.
blocks.explain: A handoff makes the client self-sufficient.
blocks.hint: What will the client need on day one?

checklist: I listed every account and who owns it
I know to keep client data in the client's accounts
